chunks: A number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Muhammad ibn Hakim, from Muhammad ibn Muslim who said:

I heard Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) saying: 'Among some of what God revealed from His Books was: "I, I am God! There is no god except Me. I created the good and I created the evil. So beatitude is for the one upon whose hands I cause the good to flow, and woe be upon the one upon whose hands I cause the evil to flow, and woe is for the one who says, "How is this so" and "How is that so."'

key_terms.أَجْرَيْتُ عَلَى يَدَيْهِ: I caused to flow upon his hands — metaphor for God using a person as an instrument for good or evil
key_terms.الْخَيْرَ وَالشَّرَّ: Good and evil — referring to the ontological reality of both as God's creation, addressing the problem of evil in Islamic theology
key_terms.طُوبَى: Beatitude, blessedness, felicity — a Quranic term (13:29) referring to a blessed state or tree in Paradise
key_terms.وَيْلٌ: Woe, destruction, calamity — a Quranic expression of divine displeasure and impending punishment

ai.seo_question: What did Imam al-Baqir (AS) say about God creating both good and evil?
ai.summary: This hadith narrated by Muhammad ibn Muslim from Imam al-Baqir (AS) records a divine statement from God's revealed Books asserting absolute divine sovereignty over the creation of both good and evil. The hadith addresses the theological question of divine decree (qadar), affirming that God is the ultimate creator of both good and evil — not in a moral sense that encourages evil, but in the ontological sense that nothing occurs outside divine will. The final warning is directed at those who question divine decree, reflecting the early Shia theological position that accepting God's absolute decree without excessive questioning is part of true faith.
